newsitem.title: USA: U.S. faults China for lack of action on WTO entry.
newsitem.headline: U.S. faults China for lack of action on WTO entry.

text.p: Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said Thursday that China was failing to take "serious" action to join the World Trade Organisation, despite Beijing's expressed desires to be a part of the global trading forum.

Barshefsky told a Seattle business group that Chinese officials were "just treading water" on the issue of joining the WTO and that there has been no real movement in Beijing's position for a couple of years.
She made her remarks to the Seattle group as China's Trade Minister Wu Yi was in Washington, D.C., discussing a number of trade issues with Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor and other U.S. officials.
The two sides are expected to cover a wide range of trade issues including a long-running dispute over U.S. wheat exports to China.

China has refused to accept U.S. wheat that contains TCK smut, a fungus, on the grounds that the wheat might infect domestic crops. But U.S. officials say there is no danger because the wheat is milled and consumed far from China's wheat region.
Kantor said he did not expect a resolution of the dispute during this week's meetings.
Chinese textile exports to the United States and copyright protection and a recent agreement aimed at curbing piracy in China are also expected to be part of the discussions.

"They have not shown a serious intent in getting into the WTO," Barshefsky told the business group. Beijing, which wants to guarantee markets for its rapidly growing export economy, has expressed a strong desire to join the global trading system and Washington, eyeing the huge potential of the Chinese market, has said it wants China in the WTO.
But Washington wants Beijing to undertake a number of economic reforms that would open its markets to more foreign goods as a condition to joining the WTO.

China has said it wants to be part of the trading system under the more lenient rules given developing countries. But U.S. officials say China's economy is just too big to give it developing country benefits.

Barshefsky said that China's lack of action reflects domestic political wrangling over economic reforms and a concern that some state-owned enterprises may not be able to compete with foreign products.

The issue is important for Washington, because the U.S. trade deficit with China has grown rapidly in recent years and is now second only to the U.S. deficit with Japan, which was $60 billion last year.
The U.S. deficit with China hit $34 billion in 1995 and reached nearly $20 billion during the first seven months of 1996.
U.S. officials have said the deficit reflects a lack of U.S. access to China's growing markets.
